newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: PRESSURE MOUNTS ON S.AFRICAN GOVT OVER FUNDING ROW.
newsitem.headline: PRESSURE MOUNTS ON S.AFRICAN GOVT OVER FUNDING ROW.

text.p: The South African government came under increasing pressure at the weekend to name a mystery backer bailing out Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma from a foreign aid spending scandal.
The government's Auditor General, Henri Kluever, joined persistent calls by opposition parties for the backer to be named, saying he would have to be told the donor's identity under treasury rules.

Kluever told reporters he did not believe the donor's name should be kept secret. "I can hardly think of circumstances where that might be the case. Why the minister is spinning it out, I don't know."

The funding row erupted earlier this year when it emerged that Zuma had approved a 14 million rand ($3.1 million) subsidy, using European Union aid, for a Broadway-style musical "Sarafina II" intended to encourage safe sex.
When opposition parties objected that this was a waste of scarce resources, the public protector began an investigation that reported in June that Zuma had misled parliament.

At the time Zuma rejected opposition demands that she resign but announced that government support for the play would be withdrawn and that the EU, whose money had been used without its knowledge, would get its aid back.

Last week Zuma told the public protector, Selby Baqwa, the name of a white businessman whom she said had pledged to contribute about 10 million rand to cover the government's contractual obligations on condition he was not named publicly.

Baqwa told reporters that he accepted Zuma's guarantees on the donor, and did not see the necessity of naming him. "It was obvious to me that the white businessman was the source. There was no agency being suggested," he added.
But two Sunday newspapers reported at the weekend that the businessman named by Zuma was a front man for the real donor.
The Sunday Times said the contribution was being channeled through a 500 million rand investment company, SAM-Sikonke.
Vivian Reddy, a millionaire friend of Zuma's, is chairman of the investment company. He has declined comment on the report.
The Sunday Independent newspaper did not name the donor but said public speculation over his identity had reached such intensity that even President Nelson Mandela was being touted as the backer.

Slamming the secrecy surrounding the affair, it asked: "Just who is the mysterious businessman? The health minister thinks we should not be told and, astonishly in this transparent society, the public protector agrees with her."

The National Party (NP) also renewed its call on Sunday for Mandela to sack Zuma for pursuing the Sarafina II production instead of switching her ministry's focus to a cheaper, and more effective, communication campaign against AIDS.

"In the interests of thousands of South Africans who might perhaps die of AIDS, President Mandela is now requested to replace Dr Zuma immediately with a more competent Minister of Health," party spokesman Jan Bosman said in a statement.
Mandela has repeatedly defended Zuma as a very good minister and has advised her critics to resolve their problems by sitting down to talk to her.
